transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-02-21 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Olivia Park (Redwood SE) — Rafael Ortiz, Priya Menon, Daniel Kim, Alexei Moroz (Skyward Solutions)

Summary: quick discovery to validate Skyward's requirements for a private/VPC-only deployment of Redwood (they want to avoid public internet egress and need EU data residency for certain products). Discussed PrivateLink vs VPC peering, Transit Gateway considerations, NAT/egress IP strategy, KMS integration, audit logging, and testing/rollout plan.

Topics: private endpoints, region gating, dedicated vs hosted, egress IPs, SOC2/audit, KMS/HSM, canary rollout, peering vs privatelink, multi-account AWS orgs.

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Jordan Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:04] Rafael Ortiz: yep, loud and clear, thanks Jordan. Rafael here.
[00:07] Priya Menon: Priya on sec team. we'll be listening for encryption and audit stuff.
[00:10] Maya Singh: great, Maya from Redwood, SE. I'll try to cover the network patterns and run through constraints as we go.
[00:15] Alexei Moroz: Alexei, product, just curious about latency and regional gating mostly.
[00:20] Jordan Patel: to kick us off, quick goal check: looks like you want a private-only deployment in AWS, no public endpoints, and certain workloads must stay in eu-west-1 and be onshore. is that right Rafael?
[00:29] Rafael Ortiz: yes, exactly. we have two classes: internal agent tooling can touch hosted endpoints in the us, but customer-facing chat must be EU-only. and we need static egress IPs so our DLP and IP allowlists work.
[00:41] Daniel Kim: plus we run across three AWS accounts: infra, dev, and prod, and we'd prefer Redwood to exist in prod account or a transit account with peering.
[00:49] Maya Singh: perfect. so there are a couple of patterns we typically recommend: interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) to a managed NLB per model service, or VPC peering/transit gateway where Redwood's VPCs peer into your network. each has tradeoffs around cross-account routing and IP management.
[01:05] Priya Menon: quick question — does Redwood support PrivateLink with KMS integration? we need keys to be customer-managed.
[01:10] Olivia Park: yes, we support customer KMS for encryption-at-rest in Private deployments. there is an HSM option for Private installs but for hosted/dedicated we'd do CMKs via KMS. slight note: our docs sometimes say "K M S" in auto transcripts.
[01:21] Rafael Ortiz: okay, good. on the IP side, do you surface a pool of static egress IPs per deployment? we can't have ephemeral addresses.
[01:28] Maya Singh: for Redwood Private we can allocate fixed egress IPs via NAT gateways in the provider VPC, or we can front with Elastic IPs behind a set of NLBs if you're using PrivateLink. with peering, egress comes from your side so you control the outbound addresses.
[01:43] Daniel Kim: so if we do PrivateLink, Redwood's egress would still hit our NAT, correct? I think we want outbound to appear from our NAT so the DLP sees it.
[01:50] Jordan Patel: yes, most customers do PrivateLink->NAT on their side so outgoing calls go over your own egress. Redwood only needs to allow the interface endpoints to talk to our NLB.
[01:58] Alexei Moroz: what about latency? is PrivateLink slower than peering?
[02:03] Maya Singh: typically negligible difference. the main latency components are cross-AZ and the model runtime itself. peering can simplify routing but you hit more management complexity across accounts.
[02:12] Rafael Ortiz: we also have a Transit Gateway already in prod, do you have experience connecting Redwood to a TGW?
[02:18] Maya Singh: yes, many customers use TGW. Redwood can attach to a TGW in a shared networking account — we provide route table guidance. caveat: if you have strict prefix lists and AWS Network Firewall there are additional steps, we can share a runbook.
[02:30] Priya Menon: on compliance: SOC2 is required and we need packet-level audit logs for requests touching PII. does Redwood capture request-level audit trails?
[02:38] Olivia Park: we capture detailed per-request logs in Private — request IDs, model version, prompt metadata (customer-configurable). for PII we recommend using our redact-before-store hooks, and you can forward logs to your SIEM via Kinesis or S3 with encryption.
[02:51] Daniel Kim: any chance of running Redwood on our on-prem racks? we have a partially air-gapped cluster for EU workloads.
[02:57] Maya Singh: we do an on-prem package for fully air-gapped customers but that's a longer engagement with professional services. for most teams, VPC Private deployment in a cloud region is faster.
[03:06] Rafael Ortiz: understood. for the EU requirement, we need data residency in eu-west-1 and backups to remain within the EU. can Redwood guarantee regional-only storage?
[03:14] Jordan Patel: yes, you can pin model data and state to a region in Redwood Private. backups and logs can be configured to stay in the same region and be placed in your customer-managed S3 buckets.
[03:23] Alexei Moroz: do you do model failovers across regions? like if eu-west-1 has an outage, what's the failover story?
[03:29] Maya Singh: by default we respect pinned regions. for critical apps you can set a fallback region but that would require legal review because data may cross boundaries. we can set cross-region replication disabled for EU-only datasets.
[03:40] Rafael Ortiz: ok, good. about onboarding: how much configuration does our infra team need to do? we have limited cycles.
[03:46] Olivia Park: we'll provide terraform modules and an example CloudFormation template for PrivateLink or TGW attachments. Maya can share a minimal checklist that Daniel can run in a sandbox.
[03:55] Daniel Kim: sounds good. one technical nit — what's the required MTU and are there any jumbo frame requirements for KV cache syncing?
[04:02] Maya Singh: no jumbo frames required. typical MTU 1500 is fine. our KV cache uses small packets and continuous batching; big frames don't help much. occasionally the docs say KV cache as K V cache — ignore that.
[04:12] Priya Menon: for SSO and RBAC, we want SAML + SCIM provisioning. supported?
[04:16] Jordan Patel: yes, SAML SSO and SCIM user provisioning supported for Redwood Console and private control plane. we also integrate with Okta and AAD.
[04:23] Rafael Ortiz: any known gotchas with security groups and ports? we prefer to limit access to a narrow CIDR.
[04:28] Maya Singh: we document a small set of ports — typically 443 for everything, and ephemeral ports for intra-cluster comms which are over the peering/VPC link only. if you're using PrivateLink, it's all over TLS on port 443.
[04:38] Daniel Kim: about the rollout, we need to run a pilot for 2 weeks with canary traffic. does Redwood support weight-based routing to older models if a regression happens?
[04:46] Olivia Park: yes our rollout tooling supports canary/A-B style rollouts and automatic fallbacks. you can configure traffic split and request-based checks.
[04:52] Alexei Moroz: good. budget question: roughly, how does dedicated vs private compare? we're evaluating both.
[04:58] Jordan Patel: quick primer: Dedicated is reserved Redwood capacity in our hosted environment — easier to run and cheaper ops but data touches Redwood-managed infra. Private gives you full VPC isolation and region pinning but requires more networking work and an enterprise contract. we can share an apples-to-apples pricing sheet.
[05:12] Priya Menon: would Dedicated satisfy our EU residency needs?
[05:15] Maya Singh: sometimes — we have dedicated clusters in EU regions but customers who need strict control prefer Private where the control plane can be customer-managed. it's a compliance conversation.
[05:24] Rafael Ortiz: ok, operational question: how do we rotate KMS keys and ensure the Redwood service continues to operate?
[05:30] Maya Singh: key rotation is supported. we recommend a roll plan: rotate CMK, validate data access in a staging instance, then rotate in prod. Redwood also supports key access checks and audit logs to confirm decrypt operations.
[05:41] Daniel Kim: we use strict egress allowlists — can you provide a list of IPs/domains Redwood will call for software updates or metrics?
[05:47] Olivia Park: yes we will provide an egress whitelist and also an allowlist for our internal monitoring collectors; for Private deployments you can opt to route telemetry to your endpoint instead of ours.
[05:58] Rafael Ortiz: one more networking question — can Redwood live in a shared services account and expose endpoints to multiple application accounts?
[06:04] Maya Singh: yes that's a common pattern: Redwood in a central networking account with TGW and spokes for each app account. you will need route propagation and correct security groups. we'll provide a sample multi-account architecture diagram.
[06:16] Priya Menon: please also include steps for firewall inspection and how to prevent token exfiltration in those diagrams.
[06:21] Jordan Patel: absolutely. we'll include recommended header redaction and a sample WAF rule set.
[06:26] Rafael Ortiz: on timelines, we want to pilot in two weeks and be in prod within eight weeks if the pilot goes well. is that feasible?
[06:33] Jordan Patel: feasible, yes — pilot (2 weeks) + integration (2–4 weeks) + compliance signoff and scale (2–4 weeks). depends on your internal approvals.
[06:43] Daniel Kim: ok Daniel to do network discovery work and share CIDR map and TGW config by Friday.
[06:49] Jordan Patel: perfect. Maya and Olivia will compile the network checklist and SOC2 pack and share by Thursday.
[06:55] Alexei Moroz: thanks all, last Q: are there examples of customers with similar constraints?
[06:59] Maya Singh: yes, we've worked with two EU banks and a healthcare provider on similar EU-only Private onramps — we can anonymize references.
[07:07] Rafael Ortiz: that's helpful. thanks everyone.
[07:09] Jordan Patel: ok we'll recap in the follow-up mail. thanks for your time.
